'''Kenneth W. Wachter''' (born January 13, 1947) is an American mathematical [[Demography|demographer]] and [[statistician]], known for contributions to demographic microsimulation ([[agent-based model]]ing), [[anthropometric history]], statistical [[endocrinology]], and evolutionary [[biodemography]].<ref name="Department of Demography">{{Cite web |title=Kenneth Wachter |url=https://www.demog.berkeley.edu/faculty/kenneth-wachter-2/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |website=Department of Demography |language=en-US}}</ref> He is [[Distinguished professor|Distinguished Professor]] [[Emeritus]] of [[Demography]] and [[Statistics]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name="Department of Demography" /> Wachter was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1999.<ref name="National Academy of Sciences Member Directory">{{Cite web |title=Kenneth W. Wachter |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/kenneth-w-wachter-jfrljz/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |website=National Academy of Sciences Member Directory}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Wachter was born in [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn, New York City]], and grew up in [[Westfield, New Jersey]].{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} He is the son of [[lawyer]] John H. Wachter and [[columnist]] Evelyn Ardelle Sidman.<ref name="Marquis Who's Who-2010">{{Cite book |last=Marquis Who's Who |url=http://archive.org/details/whoswhoinamerica00mar_ric |title=Who's who in America, 2011 [electronic resource] |date=2010 |publisher=New Providence, N.J. : Marquis Who's Who |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-1-84972-979-6}}</ref> He attended The [[Pingry School]] in Elizabeth, [[New Jersey]], and was named a Presidential Scholar by President [[Lyndon B. Johnson]] in 1964.<ref name="National Academy of Sciences Member Directory" /> He earned his [[Bachelor of Arts]] magna cum laude in [[History]] and [[Literature]] from [[Harvard College]] in 1968, where he was elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]] in his junior year<ref>{{Cite web |title=Phi Beta Kappa Selects Junior 8 {{!}} The Harvard Crimson |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1967/4/14/phi-beta-kappa-selects-junior-8/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |website=www.thecrimson.com |language=en}}</ref> and awarded the Harvard Prize for History and Literature.<ref name="National Academy of Sciences Member Directory" />

As a Keasbey Memorial Scholar, Wachter attended graduate school in the [[United Kingdom]]. In 1971, while working as a [[Research fellow|Research Fellow]] at [[St Catherine's College, Oxford]], he was awarded a [[Master of Arts]] by special decree in [[Applied mathematics|Applied Mathematics]] from the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name="Department of Demography" /> He completed his doctorate in [[statistics]] at [[Trinity College, Cambridge|Trinity College]], [[University of Cambridge]], in 1974. His [[Thesis|doctoral dissertation]] was titled "Foundations of the Asymptotic Theory of Random Matrix Spectra".<ref name="Department of Demography" />

== Career ==
Wachter worked at [[Bell Labs|Bell Telephone Laboratories]] as an Associate Member of technical staff in the early years of his career (1968–1969).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kenneth W. Wachter — Harvard University Press |url=https://www.hup.harvard.edu/authors/8225-wachter-kenneth-w |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20251215194519/https://www.hup.harvard.edu/authors/8225-wachter-kenneth-w |archive-date=December 15, 2025 |access-date=October 7, 2026 |website=Harvard University Press |language=en}}</ref> Wachter became a Miller Fellow in [[Statistics]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1977.<ref name="Department of Demography" />

In 1978, Wachter was a founding member of the newly reconstituted department of [[Demography]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he taught throughout his career.<ref name="Marquis Who's Who-2010" /> Under the leadership of Eugene Hammel, Ronald D. Lee, and Wachter, the [[University of California, Berkeley|Berkeley]] [[Demography]] Department fostered [[Mathematics|mathematical]] and formal [[demography]], macro-level economic and [[historical demography]], interdisciplinary [[qualitative research]], [[biodemography]], and [[Ageing studies|aging studies]], training some of the leading demographers of the 21st Century.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=David P. |first1=Smith |url=https://www.demogr.mpg.de/books/drm/011/978-3-642-35858-6_Book_Online.pdf |title=Mathematical Demography: Selected Papers |last2=Keyfitz |first2=Nathan |date=2013 |publisher=Springer / Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research |isbn=978-3-642-35857-9 |edition=2nd |volume=11 |location=Heidelberg |publication-date=2013 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-35858-6}}</ref> From 1997 to 2008, he chaired the Department of Demography. From 2009 to 2010, he was named Miller Professor at the [[Miller Institute]] for Basic Research in Science. He has been a Professor of the Graduate School and [[Distinguished professor|Distinguished Professor]] [[Emeritus]] since 2014.<ref name="Department of Demography" />

== Leadership and public advisory roles ==
Wachter was an expert witness for the U.S. Department of Justice's Civil Division and a member of the Secretary of Commerce's Special Advisory Panel on Census Adjustment from 1989 to 1991.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Freedman |first1=David A |last2=Wachter |first2=Kenneth W. |date=2001 |title=Census Adjustment: Statistical Promise or Statistical Illusion |url=https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~census/596.pdf |journal=Society |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=26–33 |doi=10.1007/s12115-001-1011-8 |doi-broken-date=October 7, 2026 }}</ref> In addition to serving on the [[Editorial board|Editorial Board]] of the Proceedings of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] covering [[social science]]s from 2000 to 2006 and starting in 2010, he chaired the Scientific Advisory Committee of the [[Max Planck Institute]] for [[Demography|Demographic]] Research in [[Rostock|Rostock, Germany]] from 1999 to 2004 and the Committee on Population of the National Research Council from 2003 to 2008.<ref name="National Academy of Sciences Member Directory" />

Additionally, he was a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] Committee on Publications (2015–2023), the [[Board of directors|Board of Directors]] of the [[Population Association of America]] (1999–2002), and the [[Board of directors|Board of Directors]] of the [[Social Science Research Council]] (1993–2000).<ref>{{Cite web |title=PAA Officers & Board Members - Population Association of America |url=https://www.populationassociation.org/about/officers-directors/past-board |access-date=October 7, 2026 |website=www.populationassociation.org |language=en}}</ref>

== Research ==
In 1971, with [[Peter Laslett]] and Eugene Hammel, Wachter developed the SOCSIM [[Demography|demographic]] [[microsimulation]] program, the first to track [[kinship]] through parents of both sexes with rates changing over time,<ref>{{Cite book |url=http://archive.org/details/worldwehavegaine0000unse |title=The World we have gained : histories of population and social structure |date=1986 |publisher=Oxford, UK ; New York, NY, USA : B. Blackwell |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-631-13871-6}}</ref> a [[prototype]] for the agent-based models that have become common in social science. Beginning with ''Statistical Studies of Historical Social Structure'' (1978), SOCSIM has been applied to a host of problems in [[kinship]] forecasting, [[Population structure (genetics)|population structure]], [[incest taboo]]s, [[Race (human categorization)|race]] and family, [[orphan]]hood, and bereavement.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zagheni |first=Emilio |date=2015 |title=Microsimulation in Demographic Research |url=https://www.zagheni.net/uploads/3/4/4/7/34477700/microsimulation_in_demographic_research.pdf |website=Elsevier}}</ref> It is one of the few creations from the early days of scientific computing still in use after fifty years.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kotschy |first1=Rainer |last2=Suarez Urtaza |first2=Patricio |last3=Sunde |first3=Uwe |date=October 20, 2020 |title=The demographic dividend is more than an education dividend |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=117 |issue=42 |pages=25982–25984 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2012286117 |doi-access=free |pmc=7584873 |pmid=33020314}}</ref>

''Height, Health, and History'' (1990) by [[Roderick Floud]], Annabel Gregory, and Wachter opened up the use of stature to estimate changes in living standards, analyzing English military and charity measurements of heights from the 1700s onward.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://www.nber.org/books-and-chapters/height-health-and-history-nutritional-status-united-kingdom-1750-1980 |title=Height, Health, and History: Nutritional Status in the United Kingdom, 1750-1980 |last1=Floud |first1=Roderick |last2=Wachter |first2=Kenneth |last3=Gregory |first3=Annabel |date=January 1, 1990 |publisher=National Bureau of Economic Research |language=en}}</ref> In the 1980s, Wachter partnered with Dr. George R. Merriam III to develop the PULSAR approach to peak detection in episodic [[hormone]] secretion series,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Merriam |first1=G. R. |last2=Wachter |first2=K. W. |date=1982 |title=Algorithms for the study of episodic hormone secretion |url=https://journals.physiology.org/doi/abs/10.1152/ajpendo.1982.243.4.E310 |journal=American Journal of Physiology-Endocrinology and Metabolism |publisher=American Physiological Society |volume=243 |issue=4 |pages=E310–E318 |doi=10.1152/ajpendo.1982.243.4.E310 |pmid=6889816 |issn=0193-1849}}</ref> which has continued in use among [[Endocrinology|endocrinologists]] into the 2020s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Curran-Everett |first=Douglas |date=2005 |title=Estimation of dose-response curves and identification of peaks in hormone pulsations: classic marriages of statistics to science |url=https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/classicessays.00034.2005 |journal=American Journal of Physiology Endocrinology and Metabolism |publisher=American Physiological Society |volume=289 |issue=3 |pages=E363–E365 |doi=10.1152/classicessays.00034.2005 |pmid=16091391 |issn=0193-1849}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Porteous |first1=Robert |last2=Haden |first2=Patricia |last3=Hackwell |first3=Eleni C. R. |last4=Singline |first4=Aaron |last5=Herde |first5=Michel K. |last6=Desai |first6=Reena |last7=Handelsman |first7=David J. |last8=Grattan |first8=David R. |last9=Herbison |first9=Allan E. |date=November 1, 2021 |title=Reformulation of PULSAR for Analysis of Pulsatile LH Secretion and a Revised Model of Estrogen-Negative Feedback in Mice |journal=[[Endocrinology]] |volume=162 |issue=11 |article-number=bqab165 |doi=10.1210/endocr/bqab165 |issn=1945-7170 |pmid=34383026}}</ref>

The volume ''Between Zeus and the Salmon'' (1997), edited by Wachter and [[Caleb Finch]], consolidated the new field of the [[biodemography]] of [[Ageing|aging]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Checking your browser - reCAPTCHA |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK100411/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |website=www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov}}</ref> David Steinsaltz, Steve Evans, and Wachter went on to formulate [[mathematical model]]s with rich demographic structure for the [[Evolution|evolutionary process]] of [[mutation]] accumulation, helping elucidate commonalities across species in processes of [[senescence]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wachter |first1=Kenneth W. |last2=Steinsaltz |first2=David |last3=Evans |first3=Steven N. |date=July 22, 2014 |title=Evolutionary shaping of demographic schedules |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=111 |issue=supplement_3 |pages=10846–10853 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1400841111 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=4113925 |pmid=25024186}}</ref> Wachter's textbook ''Essential Demographic Methods'' (2014) brought conceptual depth to the teaching of formal [[demography]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wachter |first=Kenneth W. |url=https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674045576 |title=Essential Demographic Methods |date=2014 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-04557-6 |location=Cambridge, MA}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
Throughout his career, Wachter has received awards for his scientific and academic contributions. He was named a [[Presidential Scholars Program|Presidential Scholar]] in 1964 and went on to be elected a Fellow of the [[American Statistical Association]] in 1986.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ASA Fellows |url=https://ww2.amstat.org/fellows/ |website=American Statistical Association}}</ref> In 1988, the [[Population Association of America]] honored him with the Mindel C. Sheps Award for Outstanding Contributions to Mathematical [[Demography]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Annual Awards - Population Association of America |url=https://www.populationassociation.org/about/annual-awards/sheps-award |access-date=October 7, 2026 |website=www.populationassociation.org |language=en}}</ref> His research and leadership earned him fellowship in both the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1997,<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 10, 2026 |title=Kenneth Willcox Wachter {{!}} American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/kenneth-willcox-wachter |access-date=October 7, 2026 |website=www.amacad.org |language=en}}</ref> followed by election as a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences|U.S. National Academy of Sciences]] in 1999.<ref name="National Academy of Sciences Member Directory" /> Beyond his research achievements, UC Berkeley's Division of [[Social science|Social Sciences]] recognized him with the Distinguished Teaching Award in 2002 and the Distinguished Service Award in 2008, alongside the Alumni "Letter in Life" Award from [[Pingry School|The Pingry School]] in 2007.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alumni Awards - The Pingry School |url=https://www.pingry.org/forever-blue/alumni/alumni-awards |access-date=October 7, 2026 |website=www.pingry.org |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
He is married to Bernadette Bell and lives in [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]] and on [[Sea Ranch, California|The Sea Ranch, California]].<ref name="Marquis Who's Who-2010" />

* Barbi, E.; Lagona, F.; Marsili, M.; Vaupel, J. W.; Wachter, K. W. (2018). ''The Plateau of Mortality: Demography of Longevity Pioneers''. ''Science''. 360 (6396): 1459–1461.
* Goldstein, J. R.; Cassidy, T.; Wachter, K. W. (2021). ''Vaccinating the oldest-old against COVID-19 saves both the most lives and the most years of life''.
